answers.justification: Ashgrove and Millbrook combined inflow did not change (5,060 vs 5,075 m³/day, C4), so no water is being lost from the system. The acoustic survey of 70% of mains found only 0.4 L/s of leaks (C2). The model study supporting a leak on section RC only tested the brief's burst scenarios (C13).

At S1, an unexplained 8.6 L/s step not caused by demand (E2, C7, C12) or the PRV (E4, C1) fits a leak. But the step happened on the same morning the Millbrook works started (E3), and Okafor's boundary check only covered GIS mains connections (E5, C6), so a temporary transfer was still a live rival.

PRV outlet held at 3.97–4.03 bar throughout, and the valve opened further to pass more flow (E4). The controller logged no alarms or setpoint changes, and the service checked the setpoint against a test gauge (C1).

The method statement specifies an overland hose from Ashgrove hydrant AG-417 to Millbrook ML-112 (C5). Millbrook night flow fell by about 8.4 L/s at 06:38–06:44 as Ashgrove's rose by 8.6 L/s at 06:40 (C4, E2). Combined inflow was unchanged (C4), and the diary records the link still connected on 3 Oct (C5).

At S1, the mains boundary valves were confirmed shut and control had no cross-feed on record (E5, C6), which counts against H3. But the step coincided with the start of the adjoining Millbrook works (E2, E3), and hydrant-to-hydrant links were not checked, so H3 could be neither established nor excluded.

Household night use was flat at 2.0 L/h (C7). Fenwick Fields allows only 0.05 L/s (C3). The heatwave demand rise ended by 14 Sept, yet the night-flow step persisted, and no other DMA stepped (E2, C12).

The diary claims control 'ok'd' the link, but the entry was written up on 4 Oct after Brannock was contacted. Against that, control logged nothing because it was busy with the Northfield burst, calls were not recorded, and the duty controller has not been interviewed (C5, C8). Okafor's 'none on record' (E5) fits either version.

The works' hose (C5) explains the link: Ashgrove's step and Millbrook's fall happen within minutes of each other (E2, C4), combined inflow is conserved (C4), and the Millbrook contacts show a cut-off followed by restoration at 06:50 (C11). Together these give mechanism, timing and covariation, with the leak rival excluded.
Outlet pressure stayed at setpoint from the 5 Sept service through the 9 Sept onset, the event log shows nothing abnormal, and the onset came four days after the service (E4, C1).
Fenwick Fields was completed on 29 Aug, not 9 Sept, and its total night allowance is 0.05 L/s against an 8.6 L/s step (C3, E3).

The Station Road main was recommissioned on 27 Sept (C5, C11), but the hose was still connected on 3 Oct (C5) and Millbrook inflow had not recovered (C4). Removing the link and checking the meters and logger addresses the cause directly and also confirms the diagnosis.

Raising the setpoint to 4.8 bar breaches the PM-7 4.2 bar cap that was set after the 2022 burst cluster in the cast-iron mains (E4). It would also push more water through the transfer rather than fix the cause (C4, C5).

Whether the contractor failed to inform control is unresolved: the diary claim is self-serving, but control's records are incomplete and the duty controller has not been interviewed (C5, C8). A formal sanction now could punish the wrong party.
Customers have been below the 2.0 bar service level since 9 Sept (E1, C9), so communicating with them is reasonable. It is not among the best actions because it does not resolve the cause (C4, C5).

The method statement and diary (C5), minute-level timing (E2, C4), the conserved combined inflow (C4), the verified meter (C15) and the null acoustic survey (C2) are enough to justify removing the Ashgrove–Millbrook link (A1).

ambiguousItems: S02: at S1 a leak is the most obvious reading of an unexplained 8.6 L/s step with boundary valves verified shut (E5), so 'supported' is defensible. 'Unknown' rests on the same-day Millbrook works start (E3).
S05: at S1, 'contradicted' is defensible from the boundary-valve check and control's 'none on record' (E5, C6). 'Unknown' rests on the timing coincidence with the Millbrook works (E3).
S14: writing to customers could be called 'preferred' as a low-cost parallel step, or only 'acceptable'.

S07: one could argue 'supported' because the permit's §7 is blank and control has no record. But the permit is open (§7 is normally completed at close-out), and control was distracted while call recording was offline, so 'unknown' fits better.
caseProblems: Timeline inconsistency: the presenting request is dated 1 Oct, but C5 includes diary entries from 3 Oct and a 4 Oct write-up. That is evidence from after the decision point, filed in stage S2, which is defined only as 'to early October'.

C4's line 'No change around 27 Sept' plus the C5 diary entry 'Overland link still connected' (3 Oct) nearly hand over the A1 answer. The C5 method statement is a near-direct statement of the hidden mechanism.
The C13 catalogue title and limitations note ('scenarios were limited to the brief') flag the model study as weak evidence fairly openly.

Minor: an 80 mm hose carrying about 8.6 L/s continuously (about 1.7 m/s) is plausible. The Ashgrove–Millbrook pressure difference is not quantified for the hydrants, but E5 suggests about 1 bar, which is adequate.

rulings.explanation: Only S1 evidence is used here (E1–E5 plus the S1 catalogue items). At that stage every rival to H1 has been checked and excluded on its own evidence. E4 and C1 show the PRV held its setpoint. E2, C3, C7 and C12 rule out demand: night use is flat and the heatwave affected every DMA. For transfer, E5 covers both channels. The mapped boundary valves were found shut and holding pressure differences (C6). Control also had no temporary cross-boundary links or works cross-feeds on record for Ashgrove or its neighbours. The blind solution says the check 'only covered GIS mains connections' and that hydrant-to-hydrant links were not checked. E5's text says otherwise: the control query was about temporary links, which is exactly where an agreed hose would be recorded. Nothing at S1 suggests control's records are unreliable; that only appears in C8, which is S2. All that is left for 'unknown' is a date-level coincidence with the Millbrook works (E3), and no path is evidenced. A sudden, lasting 8.6 L/s step, with the rivals excluded and an old, failure-prone trunk main on record (C10), supports a leak more than any rival. So 'supported' is the defensible S1 answer.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optionally, to stop misreadings like the blind solver's, add 'including any hose or hydrant links' after 'temporary cross-boundary links' in E5.

rulings.explanation: 'Contradicted' means the evidence counts against the claim; it does not have to be conclusive. At S1 a transfer was checked through both channels. The mapped boundary valves were confirmed shut and sealing (E5, C6). Network control had no temporary links or works cross-feeds on record (E5), and that record is the channel E3's standing permit condition requires. This is real evidence against H3, not a lack of evidence, so 'unknown' (evidence does not discriminate) does not fit. The blind solution relies on two points. First, that hydrant links were not checked, which misreads E5's control query. Second, the Millbrook works' timing, but E3 gives only a date and no path. Neither cancels the negative checks. C8, which weakens control's record, is S2 and cannot be used here.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optionally, make E5's control query mention hose and hydrant links explicitly, so it is clear that temporary links were covered.

rulings.explanation: E1 shows customers below the 2.0 bar service reference level since 9 Sept, with 38 contacts in the first week. By 1 Oct that is over three weeks, and nothing in the case says they have been told anything. In water-utility practice, proactive communication during a long service-level failure is standard and often expected by the regulator. It is cheap, does no harm and runs alongside A1, so a careful analyst could fairly call it 'among the best next actions' ('preferred'). The key's reason for 'acceptable' is that it does not restore pressure. That is a judgement about how strictly to read 'best'; the evidence does not force it, because the actions do not compete with each other.
rulings.fix: Add a line to E1 (or a short S1 item) saying customer services have already sent SMS and web updates to Beacon Hill and Ridgeway customers on the low pressure, for example on 16 Sept and 29 Sept. A further letter is then reasonable but adds little, so only 'acceptable' fits. Alternatively, have E6 note that A1-type removals take under a day, so a letter would arrive after recovery.

rulings.explanation: Each piece of evidence for H5 is undercut. The blank permit §7 is explained by the permit still being open, since §7 is completed at close-out (C5). Control having no record (E5, C8) is weak: from 05:52 to 09:30 the log covered only the Northfield burst, calls were connected but not recorded, and the duty controller has not been interviewed (C8). The evidence against H5 is weak too. The diary's 'Rang control — ok'd' was written up on 4 Oct, after the investigation contacted Brannock, so it is self-serving and unverified. Neither side is established, so 'unknown' is the only defensible answer. 'Supported' would treat not on record as not informed, and C8 directly undermines that inference.
